newsitem.title: USA: Food Lion rests case against ABC.
newsitem.headline: Food Lion rests case against ABC.

text.p: Grocery chain Food Lion Inc rested its case Tuesday against the ABC television network after deposition testimony from ABC producers and lawyers.

Salisbury, N.C.-based Food Lion, the U.S. unit of Belgian retailer Ets Delhaize Freres et Cie "LE LION' SA, is charging ABC and four of its producers committed tresspassing, civil fraud and other criminal offenses during an undercover investigation for a 1992 "PrimeTime Live" show.
New York-based ABC is a unit of Walt Disney Co.
The program claimed the company used unsanitary food practices and sold spoiled meat.
But Food Lion maintains the producers, working undercover at two Food Lion stores, breached a duty of loyalty when they failed to ensure all items were fresh.
The network opened its case by late afternoon, asking U.S. federal judge Carlton Tilley to dismiss the charges.

Tilley turned down ABC, saying: "Certainly there is evidence from which a jury could determine that staging took place." The producers, Susan Barnett and Lynne Dale, hid a camera in their hair and recorders under their smocks.
During previous testimony, Barnett admitted she declined to tell a supervisor about spoiled salami to prevent possible sale, although she did film it.
"(The producers) used Food Lion as a Hollywood set. They used props, they did multiple takes," Food Lion lawyer Michael Mueller said.
A jury must first find ABC liable of fraud or the other charges before a damages phase of the trial is considered.
Judge Tilley has not ruled whether or not Food Lion will be able to claim damages or how much.

On Saturday, the U.S. District Court for the middle district of North Carolina heard the grocer's argument for $1.7 billion in damages to recoup losses from the expose the network aired November 5, 1992.
Food Lion claims it lost $1.5 billion in stock value at the time of the broadcast and $233 million in profits after the broadcast.
Tilley has already ruled Food Lion cannot collect damages stemming from the broadcast unless the grocer can prove the story was false and ABC knew it.

But while Food Lion maintains the story was false, it has not made that the basis of its lawsuit. The grocer said it should be allowed to ask for losses in sales and stock value because ABC would not have had a story to broadcast if not for the allegedly fraudulent hidden-camera investigation.
ABC responded Food Lion's losses stem not from the network's methods, but from the revelation of true, embarrassing information.
